title: Kickturns, Tic-Tacs and Manuals
bigQuestion: How can a small, gentle press on the tail turn into your first real tricks?

story.title: Too Hard, Then Just Right
story.kicker: A beginner learns that the tail needs a gentle press, not a stomp.
paragraphs: Maya buckles her helmet and checks the strap under her chin. One finger fits, no more. Her wrist guards are snug. Her dad sits on a bench at the edge of the empty school blacktop. The ground is smooth and dry, and no cars come near.

Maya has watched videos of kickturns. The rider presses the back of the board, the front wheels lift, and the board swings around. It looks easy. She puts her back foot on the tail and stomps down hard.
The board shoots forward out from under her. Maya drops low and lands on her knee pads. She slides a little and stops. Her hands stay tucked in. Nothing hurts, but her heart is pounding.
Her dad brings the board back. "What happened?" he asks. Maya thinks. "I pushed way too hard," she says. "All my weight went to the back. The board had nowhere to go but out."

This time she stands on the board in the grass first. She presses the tail gently, like pressing a doorbell. The front wheels rise just a few centimeters. She turns her shoulders, and the board turns with her. She sets the wheels down softly and grins.
story.think: Why did a gentle press work better for Maya than a hard stomp?

lessons.title: Gear That Fits
lessons.mainIdea: A buckled helmet that fits, wrist guards, pads and flat shoes protect you while you learn new tricks.
reading: Before any trick, put on a *helmet*. It should sit low on your forehead, not tipped back. Buckle the strap every time. Only about one finger should fit between the strap and your chin. A helmet that wobbles cannot do its job.

Next come *wrist guards*. When people fall, they often reach out with their hands. That is why wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries. Wrist guards have hard plastic pieces that help keep the wrist from bending too far.

Knee pads and elbow pads let you slide when you fall instead of scraping. Wear flat shoes with flat rubber bottoms. Flat soles grip the board. Open sandals, boots with heels, and bare feet are not safe on a board.

words.d: a hard hat with soft padding inside that protects your head; buckle it every time
pads with hard plastic pieces that protect your wrists if you fall

look.title: The Gear Check
look.text: Picture a skater getting ready. Helmet low on the forehead, strap buckled, one finger under the chin strap. Wrist guards on both hands. Pads on both knees and both elbows. Shoes with flat rubber soles, laces tied tight.
look.prompt: Check your own gear from head to toe. What is on, and what is missing?

check.q: How should a helmet strap fit?
choices: Buckled, with about one finger of space under the chin
So loose the helmet tips back
check.why: A buckled strap with about one finger of space keeps the helmet in place.

check.q: Why are wrist guards important?
choices: They make the board go faster
Wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries
check.why: People often fall onto their hands, so wrists get hurt a lot. Wrist guards help prevent that.

check.q: Which shoes are best for skating?
choices: Flat shoes with flat rubber soles
check.why: Flat rubber soles grip the board and protect your feet.

lessons.title: A Good Practice Spot
lessons.mainIdea: Learn on ground that is smooth, dry and flat, far from cars, with a grown-up nearby.
reading: Small wheels stop fast when they hit a pebble or a crack. A smooth, flat surface lets the wheels roll evenly. Good spots include an empty blacktop, a quiet basketball court, or the flat part of a skatepark. Sweep away sticks and stones first.

Water makes the ground slippery and can ruin the small metal parts inside the wheels. So skate only when the ground is dry. Stay far from streets, driveways and parking lots, where cars move. A hill is never a place to learn.

Doctors say children ages 6 to 10 should have a grown-up watching when they skate. Children under 5 should not ride skateboards at all. A grown-up can help you choose a safe spot and can help if you fall.

words.d: the top layer of the ground you ride on, such as blacktop or concrete
to watch and help someone so they stay safe

look.title: What Children's Doctors Advise
look.text: Children younger than 5 should not ride skateboards. Children from 6 to 10 should ride only with an adult watching them.
look.cite: American Academy of Pediatrics, skateboard safety advice
look.prompt: How old are you? What does this advice mean for you?

check.q: Which place is best for learning a trick?
choices: A hill with a street at the bottom
A smooth, dry, empty basketball court
check.why: A smooth, dry, flat place away from cars lets the wheels roll evenly and safely.

check.q: Why should you not skate on wet ground?
choices: Wet ground is slippery and water can harm parts in the wheels
Wet ground makes the board heavier
check.why: Water makes the ground slippery and can ruin the small metal parts inside the wheels.

check.q: What do children's doctors say about skaters ages 6 to 10?
choices: They should have a grown-up watching
They should only skate on hills
check.why: The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that children 6 to 10 be supervised by an adult.

lessons.title: How to Fall Small
lessons.mainIdea: Falling is part of learning; crouch low, land on your pads, and roll instead of catching yourself with straight arms.
reading: Every skater falls, even the best ones. Falling is part of learning. What matters is falling small. When you feel the board slipping, bend your knees and get low. A low fall is a short fall.

Next, land on the parts with pads. Drop to your knee pads and *slide* forward. Or tuck your chin and *roll* onto your shoulder and side. Keep your arms bent and close to your body. Never catch yourself with stiff, straight arms. Locked arms send the whole force into your wrists.

Practice falling on grass before you need it. Stand up, crouch, and drop to your knees. Then try rolling sideways. If a fall makes you scared, that is normal. Take a breath and try a smaller step next.

words.d: in a fall, to land on your knee pads and skid forward to a stop
in a fall, to tuck and turn your body so it lands on your shoulder and side

look.title: Two Ways to Fall
look.text: Skater one feels the board slip, stands tall, and shoots both arms out straight. Skater two feels the board slip, bends low, drops onto knee pads, and slides with arms bent close to the chest.
look.prompt: Which skater falls small? Practice skater two's fall on soft grass.

check.q: What is the first thing to do when the board slips?
choices: Stand up as tall as you can
Bend your knees and get low
check.why: Getting low makes the fall shorter and softer.

check.q: Why should you never catch yourself with locked straight arms?
choices: The whole force goes into your wrists
It makes the board roll away
check.why: Stiff arms send the force of the fall straight into the wrists.

check.q: Where is a good place to practice falling?
check.why: Soft grass is a gentle place to practice sliding and rolling.

lessons.title: A Board Your Size
lessons.mainIdea: A board that fits your feet is easier to balance and control.
reading: Skateboards come in different widths. Width is measured across the middle of the board. Small riders often use a narrow *deck*. Grown-ups often use a wider one. A deck that fits lets your feet sit across it over the bolts.

Skate shops use names for kid sizes. A mini deck is about 7 inches wide. A mid deck is about 7.5 inches wide. A full-size deck is about 7.75 inches or wider. These are typical sizes, not rules. Your feet matter more than your age.

The *trucks* must fit the deck too. The truck's axle should be about as wide as the deck. Then the wheels sit right under the edges. Ask a grown-up or a skate shop to help you choose. Stand on the board on carpet first and see how it feels.

words.d: the flat board you stand on
the metal parts under the deck that hold the wheels and help the board turn

look.title: Typical Deck Widths
look.cite: Typical sizes from skate shop size charts; feet matter more than age
look.prompt: Which deck is the widest? Which one might fit a small rider best?

check.q: What should a deck that fits let your feet do?
choices: Sit across it over the bolts
check.why: A deck that fits lets your feet sit across it, over the bolts.

check.q: How wide should the truck's axle be?
choices: Twice as wide as the deck
Half as wide as the deck
About as wide as the deck
check.why: The axle should be about as wide as the deck, so the wheels sit under the edges.

check.q: What matters more than your age when choosing a deck?
check.why: The sizes are typical; your feet matter more than your age.

lessons.title: Tail, Nose and Bolts
lessons.mainIdea: Knowing the tail, the nose, the bolts and your front and back foot helps you follow any trick's steps.
reading: The flat board you stand on is the deck. The back end curves up. That end is the *tail*. The front end curves up too. That end is the *nose*. On many boards the nose is a little longer than the tail.
Look at the top of the deck. You will see four small screw heads near each end. These are the *bolts*. They hold the trucks and wheels to the deck. Bolts show you where to put your feet.

Some riders stand with the left foot forward. That is called regular. Others put the right foot forward. That is called goofy. Both are normal. So trick steps say front foot and back foot. Your back foot works the tail.

words.d: the back end of the deck, which curves up
the front end of the deck, which also curves up
the screws on top of the deck that hold the trucks on; they show where your feet go

look.title: Find the Parts
look.text: Set a board on the carpet. Touch the back end that curves up: the tail. Touch the front end: the nose. Count the four bolts near the tail and the four near the nose. Stand on it the way that feels natural. Which foot is in front?
look.prompt: Are you regular or goofy? Say which foot is your front foot.

check.q: What is the tail of a skateboard?
choices: The back end of the deck that curves up
The front end of the deck
check.why: The tail is the back end of the deck, and it curves up.

check.q: A rider stands with the right foot forward. What is that stance called?
check.why: Goofy means riding with the right foot forward. Both goofy and regular are normal.

check.q: Why do trick steps say front foot and back foot instead of left and right?
choices: Because left and right are hard words
Because riders can be regular or goofy
Because boards have no left side
Because only goofy riders do tricks
check.why: Regular riders lead with the left foot and goofy riders with the right, so front and back works for everyone.

lessons.title: Kickturn on the Grass
lessons.mainIdea: A kickturn means pressing the tail to lift the front wheels, turning, and setting the wheels back down.
reading: A *kickturn* is a turn on the back wheels. Start on grass or carpet so the board cannot roll. First, put the ball of your back foot on the tail. Put your front foot just behind the front bolts. Bend your knees.

Next, press the tail down gently. The front wheels lift off the ground. Lift them only a little, about the height of your shoe sole. Then turn your head and shoulders the way you want to go. Your hips and feet follow, and the board pivots on its back wheels.

Last, let the front wheels down softly. Your weight goes back to the middle of the board. Try a small quarter turn first. Then turn a little farther each time. Practice turning both toward your toes and toward your heels.

words.d: a turn made by pressing the tail, lifting the front wheels, and swinging the board on its back wheels
to turn around one point that stays in place

look.title: Kickturn, Step by Step
look.text: Step 1: Back foot on the tail, front foot behind the front bolts. Step 2: Bend your knees. Step 3: Press the tail gently. Step 4: Turn head and shoulders. Step 5: The board pivots on its back wheels. Step 6: Set the front wheels down softly.
look.prompt: On grass, act out each step slowly. Which step needs the gentlest touch?

check.q: Where does the back foot go for a kickturn?
choices: In the middle of the board
check.why: The ball of the back foot goes on the tail so it can press the tail down.

check.q: What leads the turn in a kickturn?
check.why: You turn your head and shoulders first, and your hips, feet and board follow.

check.q: Why start kickturns on grass or carpet?
choices: The board cannot roll away while you learn
Carpet makes the tail lift higher
Grass is the only legal place
check.why: On grass or carpet the board stays still, so you can learn the motion safely.

lessons.title: Kickturns While Rolling
lessons.mainIdea: Once kickturns feel easy standing still, try them while rolling slowly, and keep the tail press gentle.
reading: When kickturns feel easy on grass, move to smooth, flat ground. Have a grown-up nearby. Give one small push and roll slowly. Place your feet the same way as before. Then press, turn and set down.

One common problem is pressing the tail too hard. The front wheels fly up and the board shoots out. The fix is a softer press, just enough to lift the wheels a little. Another problem is the front foot too far forward. Then the tail will not go down. Slide the front foot back toward the middle.

Moving makes a kickturn feel different. The board wants to keep rolling straight. So keep your knees bent and your weight centered over the board. Start with quarter turns. Later try a half turn, so you roll back the other way.

words.d: with your weight balanced over the middle of the board
turning one fourth of the way around, like turning from facing a wall to facing the next wall

look.title: Problem and Fix
look.text: Problem: the board shoots out. Fix: press the tail more gently. Problem: the tail will not go down. Fix: move the front foot back from the nose. Problem: the board spins too far. Fix: turn your shoulders a smaller amount.
look.prompt: Which problem has happened to you? Try its fix three times.

check.q: What usually happens if you press the tail too hard?
choices: The board shoots out from under you
check.why: Too much weight on the tail sends the front wheels up high and the board shoots out.

check.q: The tail will not go down. What is a good fix?
choices: Move the front foot farther onto the nose
Move the front foot back toward the middle
check.why: A front foot too far forward holds the nose down. Sliding it back lets the tail drop.

check.q: What should you do before kickturning while rolling?
choices: Learn kickturns standing still on grass first
Go as fast as you can
check.why: Learning still on grass first, then rolling slowly, is the safe order.

lessons.title: Tic-Tac to Move Forward
lessons.mainIdea: A tic-tac is a string of small kickturns from side to side that moves the board forward without pushing.
reading: A *tic-tac* uses small kickturns to move forward. Stand with your feet in kickturn position on flat ground. Press the tail just enough to lift the front wheels a little. Swing the nose a small way toward your toes. Set it down.

Next, lift the front wheels again. Swing the nose a small way toward your heels. Set it down. Then go back toward your toes. Each small swing moves the board forward a bit. The name comes from the tick-tock sound and motion.

Your shoulders and arms do a lot of the work. Twist your upper body one way, and the board swings the other way. Keep the swings small and even. Big swings make the board zigzag. Tic-tacs help you learn to control the tail.

words.d: small kickturns from side to side, done one after another to move forward
the side of the board where your toes point

look.title: Tick, Tock, Forward
look.text: Picture a board on flat ground. Lift the nose, swing it toward the toe side, set it down. Lift the nose, swing it toward the heel side, set it down. Toe side, heel side, toe side. The board creeps forward like a slow pendulum.
look.prompt: Try five tic-tacs in a row. Did you move forward in a straight line?

check.q: What is a tic-tac?
choices: A string of small kickturns from side to side
A way to stop with your foot
check.why: A tic-tac is small kickturns, back and forth, that move the board forward.

check.q: What happens if your tic-tac swings are too big?
check.why: Big swings make the board zigzag instead of creeping forward.

check.q: What helps swing the board in a tic-tac?
choices: Twisting your shoulders and upper body
Pushing with your front foot on the ground
Holding the nose with your hand
check.why: Twisting your upper body one way swings the board the other way.

lessons.title: Balancing on the Back Wheels
lessons.mainIdea: A manual is rolling on only the back wheels, finding the balance point and holding it.
reading: A *manual* is like a wheelie on a bike. You roll on only the back wheels. First, practice on grass. Put your back foot on the tail and your front foot behind the front bolts. Shift your weight back slowly until the front wheels lift. Find the spot where they stay up without the tail touching.

That spot is the *balance point*. Hold your arms out to the sides. Bend your knees a little. Small moves of your hips keep you there. Then let your weight move forward again, and the nose drops back down.

Next, try it rolling slowly on flat ground. If the tail scrapes the ground, you leaned too far back. Ease your weight forward a little. If the front wheels drop fast, you need a bit more weight on the back. Count how long you hold it.

words.d: a trick where you roll on only the back wheels, with the nose up and the tail not touching
the exact spot where your weight keeps the board steady without tipping either way

look.title: Finding the Sweet Spot
look.text: Picture a seesaw with the back wheels as its middle. Too much weight back, and the tail hits the ground. Too much weight forward, and the nose drops. Somewhere in between, the nose floats. Arms out, knees soft, hips making tiny moves.
look.prompt: On grass, how many seconds can you hold the nose up before it drops?

check.q: In a manual, which wheels are touching the ground?
check.why: A manual is rolling on only the back wheels.

check.q: Your tail scrapes the ground in a manual. What should you do?
choices: Ease your weight forward a little
check.why: A scraping tail means you leaned too far back, so move your weight forward a little.

check.q: What is the balance point?
choices: The spot where your weight keeps the board steady
The highest part of the nose
check.why: The balance point is where the board stays steady without tipping.

sections.title: Why It Works and How to Practice

lessons.title: The Tail Is a Lever
lessons.mainIdea: The board works like a lever: press the tail down, the back wheels act as the pivot, and the nose goes up.
reading: A *lever* is a bar that turns around a point. A seesaw is a lever. When you press down on the tail, the board turns around its back wheels. That turning point is called the *fulcrum*. The tail goes down, and the nose goes up.

The tail is short. The rest of the board is long. So a small drop of the tail moves the nose up much farther than the tail moves down. That is why a small, gentle press is all the movement you need. A big stomp lifts the nose much too far.

Early boards were flat, with no tail. Larry Stevenson got a patent for a kicktail in 1971. A kicktail is a tail bent up. It gives your foot a place to press and lifts the nose more easily. Almost every board now has a kicktail and a bent nose.

words.d: a bar that turns around one point; pushing one end moves the other end
the point a lever turns around; on a skateboard, the back wheels
a tail bent upward so your foot can press it

look.title: Boards Change Over Time
look.cite: Skateboarding history; U.S. patent for the kicktail, granted 1971
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first store-made boards and the kicktail patent?

check.q: When you press the tail, what is the fulcrum?
check.why: The board turns around its back wheels, so they are the fulcrum.

check.q: Why does a small press on the tail lift the nose a lot?
choices: The tail is short and the rest of the board is long
The nose is made of lighter wood
The wheels push the nose up
check.why: The nose is much farther from the back wheels than the tail is, so it moves much farther.

check.q: Who got a patent for the kicktail in 1971?
check.why: Larry Stevenson's kicktail patent was granted in 1971.

lessons.title: A Little Every Day
lessons.mainIdea: Short practice on many days builds a trick better than one very long practice.
reading: Your body learns a trick by doing it many times. Each try teaches your muscles and brain a little more. Short practice on many days works better than one very long day. Ten or fifteen minutes is a good start.

Plan each practice. First, warm up by rolling slowly and doing easy kickturns. Next, work on one new skill, like the manual. Then end with something you already do well. Ending on a good try helps you feel ready for next time.

Rest is part of practice too. Tired legs wobble, and wobbly legs fall more. Stop when you feel tired or upset. Sleep also helps your brain store what you practiced. Tomorrow the trick may feel easier.

words.d: doing a skill again and again to get better at it
easy moves at the start that get your body ready

look.title: One Example Practice Week
look.prompt: How many minutes in all does this example week have? Why might Wednesday be zero?

check.q: Which plan helps you learn a trick best?
choices: One very long practice once a month
check.why: Short practice on many days helps the body and brain learn.

check.q: What is a good way to end a practice?
choices: With the hardest trick you cannot do
With something you already do well
By skipping the cool-down and running off
check.why: Ending on a good try helps you feel ready for next time.

check.q: Why is rest part of practice?
choices: Tired legs wobble and fall more, and sleep helps the brain store skills
check.why: Tired legs fall more, and sleep helps your brain store what you practiced.

review.q: What should you always do with your helmet strap?
review.why: A helmet only stays on in a fall if the strap is buckled.

review.q: In a kickturn, what lifts off the ground?
review.why: Pressing the tail lifts the front wheels so the board can pivot on its back wheels.

review.q: Which trick uses small kickturns from side to side to move forward?
review.why: A tic-tac is a string of small kickturns.

review.q: Maya stomped hard on the tail and the board shot out. What would help?
choices: A gentler press on the tail
review.why: A gentle press lifts the nose just enough without sending the board out.

choices: Rolling on only the back wheels
Spinning the board in the air
review.why: A manual is balancing on the back wheels while rolling.

review.q: In the tail-as-lever idea, what goes up when the tail goes down?
review.why: The board turns around the back wheels, so the nose rises as the tail goes down.

review.q: What is the safe order for learning a kickturn?
choices: On a hill first, then flat ground
Still on grass first, then rolling slowly
review.why: Learn standing still on grass first, then try it rolling slowly.

review.q: What is the safest way to fall?
choices: Get low and slide on your knee pads with arms bent
Stay tall and catch yourself with straight arms
Grab the board with your hands
review.why: Falling small means getting low, landing on pads, and keeping arms bent.
